transcript.text: Elena, there's a critical fact that should shape our entire defense strategy. My forensic review of the former employee's company laptop has confirmed that exactly three identified trade-secret files were copied to the device. Importantly, the review found no customer data on the device and no evidence of any additional copying beyond those three files. This significantly narrows the scope of what the plaintiff can reasonably pursue. My forensic report is awaiting final partner review and has not yet been added to the case plan, but I wanted you to have this information now so we can right-size our protective measures and push back against the broad inspection demands in the complaint.

transcript.text: Elena, I need to flag several coverage facts that will directly shape our defense plan. I've reviewed the applicable policy endorsement, and the trade-secret defense is covered — but subject to four conditions: a $75,000 self-insured retention, use of insurer-approved panel counsel, written insurer consent before any forensic vendor is engaged, and notification to the insurer as part of the approved defense plan. The endorsement is currently stored in the risk department's file and has not been attached to this matter yet. This means we need to loop in the insurer before we finalize counsel arrangements or engage any forensic vendor, and we should factor the $75,000 retention into our budgeting.
